O.outcome_detail: stakeholder experiences, influencing factors, and implementation strategies

cells.quote: The primary aim of this qualitative evidence synthesis is to summarise findings from the empirical international literature with regards to the experiences and perspectives of AAC users, their families, educators and healthcare professionals about AAC use in the classroom.
cells.note: This is a study protocol stating synthesis aims and research questions, not an empirical result; no treatment-comparison contrast or effect estimate is reported.

cells.quote: From the perspective of the AAC user, difficulties are reported in relation to the useability of devices, a high cognitive load when learning how to use a communication system, and poor physical and sensory access to devices and/or systems.
cells.note: The study protocol narratively reports difficulties from cited prior literature but does not provide a treatment comparison or effect size.

O.outcome_detail: study count for assessments of critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, communication, creative thinking, digital literacy, time management, leadership, reflection, and decision-making

cells.quote: Twenty-nine studies assessed students’ 21st -century skills, which include critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, communication, creative thinking, digital literacy, time management, leadership, reflection, and decision-making skills.
cells.note: The scoping review reports a count of studies, not a treatment-versus-comparison effect.

D.treatment: authentic assessment designs focused on digital literacy

O.outcome_detail: study count for assessments enhancing digital literacy

cells.quote: However, only five studies focused on enhancing students’ digital literacy in their AA design.
cells.note: The comparison is reported only as a subset relation within the review; no comparative learning outcome or effect estimate is reported.

O.outcome_detail: number of reviewed studies using each feedback type

cells.quote: Twenty-three studies adopted formative feedback to inform students of their learning progress, including continuous feedback embedded in portfolios (e.g., Chang, 2001), feedback on draft assignments (e.g., Colbran et al., 2017), group discussions (e.g., Kaya, 2008), workshops or tutorial activities (e.g., Allen et al., 2014), online feedback (e.g., Peng et al., 2017), peer assessment (e.g., Hussain & Al Saadi, 2019) and self-assessment (e.g., Morales & Fernández, 2019).
cells.note: The review reports study counts rather than comparative learner outcomes: 4 studies used sustainable feedback versus 23 using formative feedback.

O.outcome_detail: number of reviewed studies using each feedback type

cells.quote: Twelve studies used summative feedback to explain marking decisions and ensure quality. For example, Henderson et al. (2021) utilised online oral vivas to evaluate nursing students’ learning performance in an emergency nursing unit, followed by a critical feedback discussion between the assessor and the students to calibrate their understanding of their competence levels and the achievement of desired standards. Only four studies used sustainable feedback to empower students to become sustainable assessors and self-directed life-long learners.
cells.note: The review reports study counts rather than comparative learner outcomes: 4 studies used sustainable feedback versus 12 using summative feedback.

D.treatment: student choice and autonomy in authentic assessment
D.comparison: no reported student choice and autonomy

O.outcome_detail: presence of student choice in what, how, when or where to undertake authentic assessment

cells.quote: However, only eight studies gave students choices in what, how, when and where they take AA.
cells.note: The scoping review reports design prevalence, not a comparative effect on learner outcomes.

O.outcome_detail: presence of self-reflection in authentic-assessment design

cells.quote: Eighteen studies reported that self-reflection practices were embedded in AA to help students assess their understanding, identify strengths and areas for improvement and set goals for future learning.
cells.note: The review states that self-reflection was mostly assigned and sometimes graded, but does not report comparative learning effects.

D.comparison: students as passive users of assessment rubrics

cells.quote: When examining the users of assessment criteria for judgement, only seven studies mentioned that students were assessors through self and peer assessment (e.g., Kearney, 2014; Wakefield et al., 2023). This finding implies that students, in most cases, were passive users of assessment rubrics.
cells.note: The study reports descriptive coding across 37 empirical studies, not a comparative effect on learning or assessment accuracy; the treatment/comparison and direction are therefore inferred from the reported contrast in student assessor roles.

cells.quote: Only 3 studies (Asgarova et al., 2023; Forsyth & Evans, 2019; Spanjaard et al., 2023) addressed social issues such as active citizenship, sustainability, social awareness, responsibility and ethics, which helped to assess students’ knowledge and skills necessary to contribute to societal transformation.

cells.quote: AAC interventions had positive effects on all of the targeted behavioral outcome; however, effects were greater for communication skills than other categories of skills.
